psychodynamic-humanistic-s2.title: Do scorers agree on inkblot responses?

study.introduction: Projective tests are scored by trained clinicians. Researchers asked whether two clinicians scoring the same inkblot responses would give similar scores, and whether a person's score would be similar six weeks later.
study.participants: 60 adult volunteers (ages 20 to 64; 34 women, 26 men) recruited through a community health center in one US city. Each gave informed consent. Responses were stored under ID numbers, not names, so no one could be identified.
study.method: Each participant described what they saw in 10 standard inkblot cards. Two trained clinicians, working separately, scored every set of responses for hostility on a scale from 0 (none) to 20 (very high). Six weeks later, the same participants did the test again and one clinician scored it.
study.results: The two clinicians' hostility scores for the same responses showed only a weak to moderate positive correlation. Scores from the first and second sessions also showed a weak to moderate positive correlation.
study.discussion: The researchers concluded that hostility scores from this test were not consistent enough to use alone when making decisions about a person.

psychodynamic-humanistic-s3.title: Acceptance and admitting mistakes
psychodynamic-humanistic-s3.text: Researchers randomly assigned 80 college students to two conditions. After a hard puzzle, an experimenter said either "I appreciate you as a participant, whatever your score" (unconditional) or "I appreciate participants who score well" (conditional). Each student then checked their own answers and marked their mistakes. The graph shows the mean percentage of their actual mistakes that students marked.

plot.label: Bar graph: mean percent of own mistakes marked, unconditional 74, conditional 52 (invented data)

items.q: Maya fails her driving test. Afterward she tells friends that the examiner was unfair, the car pulled to one side, and she did not really want her license yet anyway. Which defense mechanism best explains her account?
options: Rationalization
Reaction formation
Displacement
Sublimation

why.correct: Rationalization replaces the threatening real reason (she was not ready) with comfortable excuses.
options: Right: she builds reasonable-sounding excuses that protect her self-image from the real reason she failed.
Reaction formation would mean acting the opposite of a hidden feeling, such as praising the examiner warmly.
Displacement would mean taking her frustration out on a safer target, such as yelling at a sibling.
Sublimation channels an unacceptable urge into a useful activity; nothing here is redirected into a productive goal.

items.q: After his manager criticizes him in front of coworkers, Jamal says nothing at work. At home that evening he snaps at his younger brother over a small mess. Which defense mechanism does this show?
options: Regression
Displacement
Reaction formation
Denial

why.correct: Displacement redirects a feeling from its real source to a safer target.
options: Regression is a return to childish behavior, such as a tantrum; snapping at a sibling is not a retreat to an earlier stage.
Right: anger at the manager, a risky target, is shifted onto his brother, a safer one.
Reaction formation would mean acting the opposite of his feeling, such as being extra kind to the manager.
Denial is refusing to accept a reality; Jamal does not deny that he was criticized.

items.q: Priya privately resents a new classmate who seems to outshine her. In public, Priya is warm to the point of being overly sweet to her, praising her constantly. Which concept best explains Priya's behavior?
options: Projection
Rationalization
Reaction formation
Sublimation

why.correct: Reaction formation shows the opposite of the hidden feeling, often in an exaggerated way.
options: Projection would mean believing the classmate resents Priya, putting Priya's own feeling onto her.
Rationalization is making excuses for a behavior; Priya is acting out the reverse of a feeling, not excusing an act.
Right: an unacceptable feeling (resentment) is turned into its exaggerated opposite (excessive warmth).
Sublimation would channel the resentment into a useful goal, such as practicing harder.

items.q: A student who is often tempted to copy homework constantly accuses other students of cheating, even with little evidence. According to the psychodynamic view, which defense mechanism is at work?
options: Displacement
Denial
Reaction formation
Projection

why.correct: Projection puts one's own unacceptable thoughts or urges onto other people.
options: Displacement moves a feeling to a safer target; here the student is attributing a trait, not shifting anger.
Denial would be refusing to accept an outside fact; the student is assigning a motive to others.
Reaction formation would be acting as an extreme rule follower, the opposite of the urge, rather than accusing others.
Right: the student's own unacceptable urge to cheat is seen in other people instead of in himself.

items.q: Soon after a baby sister comes home, a 6-year-old who was fully toilet trained starts wetting the bed, sucking his thumb and using baby talk. Which defense mechanism best fits?
options: Regression
Sublimation
Rationalization
Projection

why.correct: Regression is a retreat to behavior from an earlier stage when anxiety is high.
options: Right: under stress he retreats to behavior from an earlier, more comforting stage of development.
Sublimation would channel his feelings into a useful activity, such as drawing pictures for the baby.
Rationalization involves giving excuses; a young child's return to baby behavior is not an explanation.
Projection would mean claiming the baby is jealous of him, assigning his feeling to her.

items.q: Leo has strong aggressive urges that would get him in trouble at school. He trains for hours as a competitive boxer and becomes a disciplined athlete. Which defense mechanism does this illustrate?
options: Displacement
Sublimation
Reaction formation
Denial

why.correct: Sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into an acceptable, often admired, activity.
options: Displacement would aim the aggression at a weaker target, such as a younger student, which is not socially valued.
Right: an unacceptable urge is redirected into a socially valued, productive activity.
Reaction formation would make Leo unusually gentle and opposed to fighting.
Denial would mean refusing to admit any aggressive feelings at all.

items.q: A man has coughed every morning for a year and is short of breath on stairs. When his family urges him to see a doctor, he insists nothing is wrong and changes the subject. Which defense mechanism best explains his response?
options: Repression
Rationalization
Denial
Projection

why.correct: Denial blocks a threatening outside reality from being accepted.
options: Repression pushes a painful memory or impulse out of awareness; the cough is a present fact he is told about.
Rationalization would offer excuses ("it is just allergies"); he refuses to accept that there is a problem at all.
Right: he refuses to accept a threatening reality that is in plain view.
Projection would mean saying that his family members are the ones who are sick.

items.q: A father tells his son, "I love you no matter what, and I am disappointed that you lied about the broken window." From the humanistic view, which concept does the father's first statement show?
options: Reaction formation
The self-actualizing tendency
Conditional acceptance
Unconditional positive regard

why.correct: Unconditional positive regard is acceptance of the person that does not depend on behavior; the behavior can still be judged.
options: Reaction formation is a defense that hides a feeling behind its opposite; the father states his feelings openly.
The self-actualizing tendency is the son's drive to grow; the father's statement is the condition that supports it.
Conditional acceptance would make love depend on good behavior; he says he loves his son no matter what.
Right: he accepts his son as a person while still disapproving of the behavior.

items.q: A therapist shows a client a series of ambiguous drawings of people and asks her to tell a story about what is happening in each. The therapist then looks for repeated themes in the stories. Which kind of assessment is this?
options: A projective test
A survey with a Likert scale
Naturalistic observation
An experiment

why.correct: Projective tests use ambiguous stimuli, such as inkblots or pictures, on the idea that responses reveal unconscious concerns.
options: Right: an ambiguous picture invites the person to "project" her own concerns into the story (this one is a Thematic Apperception Test).
A Likert scale asks for ratings of agreement with statements; this client tells open-ended stories.
Naturalistic observation records behavior in everyday settings without intervening; here the therapist presents pictures.
An experiment manipulates a variable and randomly assigns people to conditions; one client telling stories is an assessment.

items.q: In the humanistic view of personality, what role does the self-actualizing tendency play?
options: It keeps threatening wishes out of awareness to reduce anxiety
It pushes people to grow toward their full potential when conditions allow
It measures personality through ambiguous inkblots and pictures
It explains behavior as learned through rewards and punishments

why.correct: The self-actualizing tendency is the built-in drive to grow and fulfill one's potential.
options: That describes defense mechanisms in the psychodynamic view, not a humanistic idea.
Right: humanistic theory sees people as naturally moving toward growth when they feel accepted.
That describes projective tests, which come from the psychodynamic view.
That is the behavioral view; humanistic theory stresses growth and free choice.

items.q: In the left panel of the figure, what job do defense mechanisms do?
options: They move memories from the conscious tip into long-term storage
They make unconscious wishes easier to notice and talk about
They keep threatening thoughts below the line of awareness
They let people grow toward their full potential

why.correct: The arrow from defense mechanisms points at the awareness line: they hold threatening thoughts beneath it.
options: The figure is about awareness, not memory storage; defense mechanisms protect against anxiety.
They do the reverse: they keep threatening material out of awareness.
Right: in the psychodynamic view they reduce anxiety by keeping threatening material out of conscious awareness.
Growth toward potential is the humanistic panel's self-actualizing tendency.

items.q: A teenager senses that her parents' approval depends on straight A grades. When she fails a test, she hides it and tells herself it does not count. Using the right panel, where does the humanistic chain break first?
options: At the top: her parents' acceptance depends on her behavior
At the bottom: she has no self-actualizing tendency
In the left panel: her unconscious wishes are too strong
In the middle: her parents accept her but she misreads them

why.correct: Without unconditional positive regard she must distort her experience (hiding the failure) to stay accepted, which blocks growth.
options: Right: approval with conditions replaces unconditional positive regard, so the later links fail too.
Humanistic theory assumes everyone has the tendency; acceptance with conditions is what blocks it.
The question asks about the humanistic chain, and the problem starts with conditional approval.
The scenario says the approval really does depend on grades, so the first link is missing.

items.q: A researcher wants an assessment that fits the left panel of the figure. Which choice best fits, and why?
options: A rating of how warmly a parent responds, because acceptance shapes growth
Asking what a person sees in inkblots, which may reveal hidden concerns
Counting rewards a person receives, because rewards shape behavior
Scanning brain activity, because thoughts are made by neurons

why.correct: The psychodynamic view is assessed with projective tests such as the Rorschach inkblots and the TAT.
options: Warmth and acceptance belong to the humanistic panel, not to the unconscious.
Right: projective tests come from the psychodynamic view that unconscious material shows in how we read ambiguous stimuli.
Counting rewards fits the behavioral view, which the figure does not show.
Brain imaging fits the biological view, not the iceberg model of the unconscious.

items.q: Which research method did this study use?
options: An experiment
A case study
Naturalistic observation
A correlational study

why.correct: The study measured the relationship between scorers and between sessions, which makes it correlational.
options: No variable was manipulated and no one was randomly assigned to conditions.
A case study looks in depth at one person or a few; this study compared scores across 60 people.
Participants were tested with cards in a set procedure, not watched in an everyday setting.
Right: the researchers measured how strongly two sets of scores were related, without manipulating anything.

items.q: The results raise the most doubt about which quality of this hostility score?
options: Its reliability, because scores were inconsistent across scorers and over time
Its validity, because the hostility scores did not predict who later acted aggressively
Its generalizability, because the sample was too small to matter
Its random assignment, because people were not placed into groups

why.correct: Interrater agreement and test-retest consistency are both forms of reliability; a test that is not reliable cannot be fully valid either.
options: Right: agreement between scorers and between sessions are both measures of reliability.
The study never compared scores with real behavior, so it did not test that kind of validity.
Generalizability depends on who the participants were, not mainly on sample size.
There were no groups or conditions, so random assignment does not apply here.

items.q: Write the operational definition of hostility used in this study.

why.correct: An operational definition says exactly how the variable was measured: the 0 to 20 score from the 10 cards.

specific.frame: Hostility was measured as ___, based on ___.
specific.model: Hostility was measured as a score from 0 to 20 given by a trained clinician, based on what the participant said they saw in 10 standard inkblot cards.

opdef.label: Operational definition
options: a score from 0 to 20 given by a trained clinician
how angry the person felt that day
whether the person had a history of fights

why.1: A feeling in general is the concept, not how this study measured it.
why.2: The study never recorded fights; it scored inkblot responses.

when.label: Based on
options: what the participant saw in 10 inkblot cards
a questionnaire the participant filled out

why.1: There was no questionnaire; scores came from descriptions of inkblots.

items.q: Which ethical safeguard does the summary say the researchers used, and how?
options: Debriefing, by revealing a deception at the end of the study
Random assignment, by placing participants in groups by chance
Confidentiality, by storing responses under ID numbers instead of names
Protection from harm, by screening out people with high hostility

why.correct: Name a safeguard the summary actually describes and say how it was applied: confidentiality through ID numbers (informed consent is also described).
options: The summary describes no deception and no debriefing.
Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard, and was not used.
Right: the summary says responses were stored under ID numbers so no one could be identified.
The summary does not describe any screening of participants.

items.q: What was the independent variable in this experiment?
options: The percentage of mistakes each student marked
Conditional or unconditional appreciation
How hard the puzzle was
The number of students in each group

why.correct: The independent variable is the one the researchers manipulate: unconditional versus conditional appreciation.
options: That was measured after the feedback, so it is the dependent variable.
Right: the researchers manipulated the kind of feedback and randomly assigned students to it.
Every student got the same hard puzzle, so difficulty was held constant.
Group size describes the sample, not the variable that was manipulated.

items.q: Which conclusion do these results best support?
options: Unconditional appreciation led students to mark more of their own mistakes
Conditional appreciation made students solve more of the puzzles correctly than unconditional
Unconscious hostility caused students to hide their mistakes
Students in the two conditions marked about the same share of mistakes

why.correct: Read the graph for these groups: the unconditional group marked 74% of their mistakes, the conditional group 52%.
options: Right: 74% versus 52%, as humanistic theory predicts; accepted people had less need to distort their experience.
The graph shows mistakes marked, not puzzle scores.
Nothing in the study measured unconscious hostility; the feedback condition was manipulated.
The bars differ by 22 percentage points.

items.q: In a small pilot of the unconditional condition, five students marked 5, 7, 6, 8 and 4 of their mistakes. What is the mean number of mistakes marked?

mistakes.why: 30 is the total. Divide the total by the number of students, 5.
4 is the range (8 minus 4), a measure of spread, not the mean.

items.q: Why can the researchers conclude that the type of appreciation caused the difference?
options: Because the sample was large enough to include 80 students
Because the students came from one college
Because the two variables were correlated
Because students were randomly assigned to the two conditions

why.correct: An experiment with random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion.
options: Sample size alone does not allow a causal conclusion; the design does.
A shared background limits generalizability; it does not establish cause.
A correlation alone cannot show cause; a third variable could explain it.
Right: random assignment makes the groups similar at the start, so the manipulated feedback is the likely cause.

items.q: A critic says the psychodynamic view is hard to test scientifically. Which example best supports that criticism?
options: Projective tests take a long time because they are given to one person at a time
Defense mechanisms have names that many students find hard to remember
A man who is kind to his rival can be called truly kind or using reaction formation
Unconscious processes can now be studied in the laboratory with priming tasks

why.correct: A theory that explains every possible outcome after the fact cannot be tested, because no result could contradict it.
options: Testing one person at a time is slow but does not make a theory untestable.
How easy a term is to remember says nothing about whether the theory can be tested.
Right: when any outcome can be explained after the fact, the theory makes no prediction that could be shown wrong.
This supports a modern, testable version of unconscious processing rather than the criticism.
